nodes.text: Marie Curie was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903.
Marie Curie was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911.
Marie Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.
The Nobel Prize in Physics is awarded for outstanding contributions to physics.
Physics is a natural science studying matter, energy, and their interactions.
Albert Einstein received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921.
Einstein's Nobel Prize was for his discovery of the photoelectric effect.
The photoelectric effect is a quantum phenomenon.
Quantum mechanics describes physical phenomena at the atomic scale.
Marie Curie's research focused on radioactivity.
Polonium and radium were discovered by Marie Curie.
Radioactivity is the emission of radiation from unstable atomic nuclei.
The nucleus of an atom contains protons and neutrons.
Electrons occupy orbitals around the nucleus.
Paris is the capital of France.
France is a country in Western Europe.
The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris, France.
The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889.
World War II ended in 1945.
The United Nations was founded in 1945.
The United States declared independence in 1776.
Washington D.C. is the capital of the United States.
London is the capital of the United Kingdom.
The Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone in 1876.
Thomas Edison developed a practical electric lightbulb in 1879.
Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first powered airplane flight in 1903 at Kitty Hawk.
Johannes Gutenberg invented movable type printing around 1440.
James Watt improved the steam engine in 1769, spurring the Industrial Revolution.
Karl Benz built the first practical gasoline-powered automobile in 1885.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.
Watson and Crick described the double helix structure of DNA in 1953.
Guglielmo Marconi demonstrated wireless radio transmission in 1895.
ARPANET, the precursor to the modern internet, was created in 1969.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989.
The transistor was invented at Bell Labs in 1947.
Wilhelm Roentgen discovered X-rays in 1895.
Nikola Tesla developed the alternating current (AC) electrical system in the 1880s.
Benjamin Franklin demonstrated that lightning is electrical in nature in 1752.
Louis Pasteur developed germ theory and early vaccines for cholera and anthrax.
Isaac Newton formulated three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation.
Charles Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859, introducing natural selection.
Dmitri Mendeleev created the periodic table of elements in 1869.
Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine against smallpox in 1796.
The speed of light in a vacuum is approximately 3 * 10^8 meters per second.
Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at standard atmospheric pressure.
The human body has approximately 37 trillion cells.
DNA is made of four chemical bases: adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine.
The periodic table currently contains 118 confirmed chemical elements.
Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust by mass.
The Milky Way galaxy contains approximately 200 to 400 billion stars.
The Earth is approximately 150 million kilometers from the Sun (1 astronomical unit).
The Big Bang theory states the universe began approximately 13.8 billion years ago.
Newton's First Law: an object stays at rest or in motion unless acted on by a net force.
Newton's Third Law: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
E = mc^2 is Einstein's equation relating mass and energy.
Plate tectonics theory explains continental drift and the causes of earthquakes.
The human genome contains approximately 3 billion base pairs of DNA.
Blood circulation was first accurately described by William Harvey in 1628.
Rome is the capital of Italy and was the center of the ancient Roman Empire.
Julius Caesar was a Roman general and dictator assassinated on March 15, 44 BC.
Napoleon Bonaparte became Emperor of France in 1804.
The French Revolution began in 1789 and led to the abolition of the French monarchy.
The American Civil War was fought from 1861 to 1865 between Union and Confederate states.
World War I lasted from 1914 to 1918.
The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 18th century.
The Great Wall of China was built over many centuries to protect against northern invasions.
Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt.
Alexander the Great built one of history's largest empires, dying at age 32.
The Ancient Olympic Games were first recorded in Olympia, Greece, in 776 BC.
The modern Olympic Games were revived in Athens, Greece, in 1896.
Tokyo is the capital of Japan.
Beijing is the capital of China.
Moscow is the capital of Russia.
Ottawa is the capital of Canada.
Canberra is the capital of Australia.
Cairo is the capital of Egypt.
The Amazon River is the world's largest river by water discharge.
Mount Everest, at approximately 8849 meters, is the tallest mountain above sea level.
The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean on Earth by area.
The Great Pyramid of Giza was built approximately 2560 BC as a tomb for Pharaoh Khufu.
The Magna Carta, signed in 1215, limited the power of the English king.
The Renaissance was a cultural movement that began in Italy in the 14th century.
The Silk Road was an ancient trade network connecting China to the Mediterranean.
William Shakespeare wrote approximately 37 plays, including Hamlet and Romeo and Juliet.
Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.
Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night in 1889.
Ludwig van Beethoven composed nine symphonies despite becoming deaf.
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed over 600 works before his death at age 35.
Miguel de Cervantes wrote Don Quixote (1605), considered the first modern European novel.
Homer's Iliad and Odyssey are ancient Greek epic poems foundational to Western literature.
The Taj Mahal in Agra, India, was built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in the 17th century.
Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling in Rome between 1508 and 1512.
Pablo Picasso co-founded Cubism and painted Guernica in 1937.
The FIFA World Cup is held every four years and is the world's most-watched sporting event.
The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930.
Basketball was invented by James Naismith in 1891.
A standard marathon distance is 26.2 miles (42.195 kilometers).
Chess originated in India around the 6th century AD and spread to Persia and Europe.
The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded to individuals or organizations that advance world peace.
If X won the Nobel Prize in Physics, then X made a significant contribution to physics.
If X discovered a chemical element, then X contributed to chemistry.
If X is located in city Y, and Y is in country Z, then X is in country Z.
If event A caused event B, and B caused C, then A indirectly caused C.
If two events share the same year, they are contemporaneous.
If X and Y are capitals, they belong to different countries unless specified.
If a person won multiple Nobel Prizes, they worked across multiple fields.
If X is the first person to achieve Y, no one preceded X in achieving Y.
If X invented Y in year Z, then X is credited with creating Y around year Z.
If X won the Nobel Prize in field Y, X made an exceptional contribution to field Y.
If X is the capital of country Y, X serves as the seat of government for Y.
If X wrote work Y, then Y is attributed to X as its author or creator.
If X is in continent Y and Z is a country in Y, X and Z are in the same continental region.
If X is the largest Y in group Z, then all other members of group Z are smaller than X.
If X's research led to discovery Y, and Y saved lives, X's work has humanitarian value.
If X was assassinated in year Y, X's rule or influence ended in year Y.
If X discovered element Y, element Y is associated with X in the history of chemistry.
If X invented Y and Y led to Z, then X's invention contributed to Z.
If X developed theory Y and Y was confirmed by experiment, Y is accepted scientific theory.
If X ruled country Y from year A to year B, X governed Y during that period.
If city X is in country Y and Y is in Europe, then X is a European city.
If X painted Y and Y is displayed in museum Z, Y can be seen at Z.
If X composed work Y for instrument Z, Y is typically performed on Z.
If X won prize Y in year Z, X was the recipient of Y in Z.
If X occurred in century Y, X is a historical event of the Y century.
If X is adjacent to ocean Y, X has a coastline on Y.
If country X borders country Y, X and Y share a geographic boundary.
If X is a mountain and X has the highest elevation in region Y, X is the highest peak in Y.
If X is recognized as a landmark of civilization, X has historical or cultural significance.
If X depends on technology Y and Y was invented after X, there is a logical inconsistency.
If X is the founding year of institution Y, Y did not exist before X.
If person X died before event Y occurred, X had no direct involvement in Y.
If two scientists independently discovered the same thing, the discovery is attributed to both.
If X and Y both contributed to Z, Z is a collaborative achievement.
If event X triggered event Y in the same year, X and Y are causally linked and contemporaneous.
If X is the president of country Y, X is the executive head of Y's government.
If X is an ancient structure still standing, X has survived for centuries.
If city X served as the capital of empire Y, X had strategic importance to Y.
If X's population exceeds Y's population, X is more populous than Y.
If X is named after person Y, the naming is a tribute or recognition of Y.
If X is translated from language Y to language Z, X is accessible to speakers of Z.
If X and Y fought a war and Y won, Y gained strategic control or advantage.
If X is the second-largest Y, then exactly one Y is larger than X.
If X is both a scientist and an artist, X can contribute to both domains.
If X won multiple awards in the same field, X is considered highly accomplished in that field.
If X is a scientific law, X describes a consistent, testable regularity in nature.
To find a person's scientific field: identify the category of their Nobel Prize.
To find which country a landmark belongs to: identify the city, then the country.
To chain two facts: find the shared entity and link their attributes.
To check temporal order: compare the years of two events.
To verify a multi-hop claim: trace each hop and confirm each link independently.
To identify who invented X: search for the first person credited with creating X.
To verify a historical date: cross-reference with independently documented events.
To determine the capital of a country: identify the officially designated seat of government.
To trace the origin of an invention: identify the problem it solved and the inventor credited.
To determine if X preceded Y: compare the year X occurred with the year Y occurred.
To find where a landmark is located: identify its city, then identify that city's country.
To identify someone's nationality: look for their birthplace, citizenship, or country of residence.
To attribute a discovery: find the first published or officially credited account.
To find the duration of a historical period: subtract the start year from the end year.
To find the influence of a historical figure: trace what changed after their actions.
To chain two facts about the same person: find the shared entity and link attributes.
To verify contemporaneous events: confirm they share the same year or overlapping dates.
To find the continent of a country: consult world geography knowledge.
To find the successor to a historical ruler: identify who assumed power after the reign ended.
To find the precursor to a modern technology: trace its technological lineage back to origin.
To determine if two things are related: find a shared attribute, ancestor, or causal link.
To verify a geographic fact: check the political or physical boundaries involved.
To identify the field of a scientist: look at the subject matter of their research.
To determine whether two events are causally linked: verify the proposed mechanism.
To find the location of a museum or artwork: trace its current recorded institutional home.
Two contradictory facts about the same subject cannot both be true.
A person cannot win a Nobel Prize in a field they did not contribute to.
A city can be the capital of only one country at a time.
An event cannot precede its own cause.
A person cannot be in two locations simultaneously.
Historical facts are fixed — they do not change based on interpretation.
Since 1974, the Nobel Prize cannot be awarded posthumously.
A Nobel Prize in a given year is shared by at most three co-recipients.
No two sovereign countries can legally occupy the same geographic territory simultaneously.
An ocean is not located on a continent; oceans separate land masses.
A country's official capital is determined by its own laws, not external recognition alone.
No information can travel faster than the speed of light in a vacuum.
A scientific theory cannot be simultaneously confirmed and definitively disproven.
A person cannot be their own biological ancestor.
An invention cannot predate the inventor's birth.
An event that occurred cannot be said to have not occurred.
Two different people cannot both be the sole original inventor of the same technology.
Elements in the periodic table each have a unique atomic number.
A person cannot win multiple Nobel Prizes if their work spanned only one narrow subfield.
A historical figure cannot be both the inventor and the destroyer of the same technology.

To identify an empire's capital: find the city from which the empire was governed.
To compare the size of two oceans: use surface area measurements (Pacific > Atlantic > Indian).
